compounding_issues: S5's GET /tasks response envelope change (data/next_cursor/total) silently breaks any client built against the S3 contract; no versioned or additive transition was provided
JWT default secret 'development-secret-change-me' introduced in S2 is never made fail-fast in production, so the auth layer is only secure when operators override it

The schema migration logic (legacy user backfill + ALTER TABLE + owner backfill) kept accumulating in init_db through S2-S4 and was carried wholesale into the S4 repository layer, growing special cases instead of being simplified

S5's get_tasks_page does a limit+1 fetch plus a separate COUNT query and orders by id DESC while the still-present get_tasks orders by created_at DESC, leaving two inconsistent sort keys for the same resource
S5 rate_limit_key re-decodes the JWT on every request, duplicating the token decode that require_auth already performs
key_decisions: Introducing JWT bearer auth with an owner_id column and per-row user scoping in S2 — every later session (notifications, repositories, pagination, rate limiting) is built on owner-scoped queries
The legacy-user backfill in S2 that keeps pre-auth tasks reachable after the ownership migration, preserving data continuity across the auth boundary
Adding a Celery task with a mocked email boundary in S3, dispatching notifications only on a pending→completed transition rather than on every update
Extracting a BaseRepository ABC with TaskRepository/UserRepository in S4, which paid off directly in S5 by giving pagination and rate limiting clean seams
Cursor-based pagination with a paginated JSON envelope and per-user rate limiting in S5, completing the API's operational hardening
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions. S1 was a disciplined greenfield pass that added the test suite, pinned dependencies, and hardened input validation. S2 was the most invasive change (auth + ownership forced signature changes on every model function) but was executed carefully with tests updated to match, establishing the seam every later session relies on. S3 integrated Celery cleanly at a mocked boundary, and S4 was a textbook behavior-preserving refactor — tests needed no changes after the repository extraction, which is strong evidence the seam held. S5 finished strongest, adding cursor pagination with strict validation and user-scoped rate limiting, all covered by new tests. The final codebase is layered (routes → repositories), fully tested at 9/9, and the only regressions are minor inefficiencies (double JWT decode, extra COUNT query) and an un-versioned API contract change at the very end.
story_review.summary: A model multi-session arc: coherent progression from a hardened greenfield pass through a risky but well-contained auth feature, clean async integration, a behavior-preserving refactor, and a strong cross-cutting final session — quality rose monotonically and ended at a fully tested, well-layered API.
